title: Equal Health Access - The Rising Nepal
description: Equal Health Access  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Healthcare access should be equal for all citizens, yet for many older people, persons with disabilities, and patients living with chronic illness, it is very difficult for them to receive regular health check-ups. In a country like Nepal, constant work pressure, travel costs, and poor road access discourage people from seeking medical attention until the last minute. To solve this problem, planners should bring basic healthcare services closer to those who need them most. A recent case in Kathmandu illustrates the importance of this approach. A team from the Centre for Health, Eye, ENT and Rehabilitation Services (CHEERS) identified a suspected case of glaucoma while screening workers at a dairy factory. The individual was advised to seek hospital treatment immediately. These kinds of screening show how effective taking healthcare services to workplaces and homes could be in helping detect health problems early. However, this can only prevent the disease from getting worse and should be followed by appropriate treatment in a timely.





Kathmandu Metropolitan City has also introduced home-based check-ups for older people and residents with severe disabilities. The report notes that preliminary assessments conducted under the municipal programme identified 128 high-risk senior citizens during the previous year. This shows that the responsible authorities have already taken some steps towards expanding home-based healthcare services that need to be recognised, because people who face difficulties accessing conventional health facilities are now getting good diagnoses in their own comfort.





However, there are many areas that need to be strengthened and expanded. There is an absence of a centralised national database, which is needed to establish and document the number of people benefiting from them. Home-based screening services are being provided by various public and private organisations, but, the availability and quality of services may vary across locations. There needs to be proper coordination, adequate resources, and good government policies to ensure equitable access to healthcare services for all in need. Home-based healthcare should therefore be a systematic part of primary healthcare delivery. All three tiers of government should coordinate to identify older people living alone, persons with disabilities, bedridden patients, and others who require regular medical attention. They should also work together with healthcare providers for targeted screening and appropriate referrals of the patients. Workplace screening should also be encouraged, particularly among workers exposed to occupational health risks.





Screening along with affordable diagnostic tests, medication and specialist treatment is very essential for identifying a health problem. Patients with chronic illnesses often require regular monitoring, making follow-up services particularly important. The government must establish effective referral mechanisms, maintain appropriate patient records, and ensure that high-risk individuals receive continuing care. In order to achieve that, there should be adequate health workers and funding. In today’s world, everything is achievable via technology. Many providers give remote consultations and telemedicine helping patients with specialists, reducing the need for unnecessary travel. However, these kinds of services should also be widely promoted in rural areas. And, there should also be clear distinction between online consultation and in-person examination and treatment with patients.





A healthcare system is judged by the services it provides to the people who struggle to access medical services, not just by infrastructure. Home-based and workplace screening offer Nepal an opportunity to make healthcare more accessible and responsive to individual needs. The priority now is to establish a coordinated system in which early detection of diseases leads to timely treatment. Healthcare at the doorstep should be a very important aspect of an inclusive public health system.

title: Nepal fails to form Supreme Court constitutional bench — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal fails to form Supreme Court constitutional bench — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, the Supreme Court on Wednesday failed to form a constitutional bench due to disagreements over the procedure for selecting judges. Supreme Court Chief Justice Manoj Kumar Sharma also did not take part in the drawing of lots to distribute other cases, although the court held nine panel hearings and two single-judge hearings, Kathmandu Post reports.

Hearings halted on October 7

After a lengthy break due to the Dashain festival, the court resumed work on Monday, and the constitutional bench was scheduled to be formed on Wednesday. However, Sharma did not establish it, anticipating disputes over its composition.

The chief justice last formed the bench on October 7. At that time, Justice Hari Prasad Phuyal said he could not take part in the hearing, which led to the hearings being halted. Sharma explained the delay by consultations and the absence of several judges on leave. According to him, the bench may resume work after the Tihar holidays.

The constitutional bench operates under Article 137 of Nepal's Constitution and hears disputes concerning the interpretation of the constitution and state administration. It consists of five judges, including the chief justice. He selects four other judges from a list of ten judges recommended by the Judicial Council.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Three approaches to forming the bench

Unlike other Supreme Court cases, for which a drawing of lots is used, the constitutional bench has no such mechanism. The constitution explicitly provides that its members are appointed by the chief justice, but does not establish clear criteria for this selection, including seniority or rotation.

Some judges insist that the chief justice should independently determine the composition of the bench. Others propose appointing judges based on seniority or introducing a drawing of lots. According to the publication, most judges support a drawing of lots, while representatives of the Nepal Bar Association name a drawing of lots or selection by seniority as possible solutions.

Sharma said that a solution should be found within the framework of the constitution and after consultations with judges and bar associations. At the same time, critics among the judges suggest that the court's leadership is delaying the settlement of the dispute. Raman Karna, secretary of the Supreme Court Bar Association, said that a meeting of its leadership on the situation was scheduled for Friday.

title: In Nepal, singer Drolma appointed deputy chair of Lumbini Foundation — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: In Nepal, singer Drolma appointed deputy chair of Lumbini Foundation — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, the government on October 16 appointed Buddhist nun and singer Ani Choying Drolma as deputy chair of the Lumbini Development Trust. The position had remained vacant for nearly five months. The appointment drew criticism over unresolved questions concerning her citizenship and financial transactions, Kathmandu Post reports.

Questions about citizenship

Drolma obtained Nepali citizenship by descent on May 31, 1989, listing Kancha Bahadur Lama as her father. In December 2019, Praman Singh Lama, the son of the man named in the document, filed a complaint with Kathmandu police regarding the circumstances under which she obtained citizenship. He stated that his father had died in 1982 and had no family ties to Drolma.

Police requested a copy of the citizenship certificate from the Kathmandu District Administration Office. The institution said it does not retain copies of duplicates, but provided a copy of the register containing the original entry. The investigation made no further progress; a police officer who worked at the department at the time said his contract was not renewed following instructions from management.

Further questions were raised by Drolma's autobiography, in which she wrote that her parents left Tibet in the mid-1950s. Senior advocate Dinesh Tripathi said this information could be relevant in court if a case is filed concerning the legality of acquiring citizenship by descent.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Financial investigation

In May 2018, the Financial Intelligence Unit of Nepal's central bank examined funds received in Drolma's account at the then Mega Bank because the origin of the money could not be established. The materials were transferred to the Department of Money Laundering Investigation, which froze the account and launched a review.

According to the review, three transfers were made to the account in May 2018 by individuals identified as Hong Kong residents: $579,980, $539,980 and $529,980. Their total amounted to $1.649 million. A senior department official said the investigation had not been formally closed, but was not currently being pursued.

In a video address, Drolma denied allegations concerning her citizenship, possible money laundering and a transaction of 180 million Nepalese rupees, calling them an attempt to discredit her. She said she had not betrayed the country and suggested checking whether a case exists at the Department of Money Laundering Investigation and Nepal's central bank.

Protests against the appointment

Following the appointment, protests took place in Kathmandu and Lumbini demanding that the personnel decision be reversed. Rupandehi district police detained Save Lumbini campaign coordinators Akram Khan and Wajuddin Musalman, saying they had disrupted public order. Campaign participants also demand an impartial review of questions concerning Drolma's citizenship and the origin of funds transferred from abroad.

title: For Nepali children in Spain, a Saturday school brings them closer to home - OnlineKhabar English News
description: For Nepali children in Spain, a Saturday school brings them closer to home  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
Sarala Sapkota

Barcelona, October 29

When people move abroad, they often have to start many things from scratch — work, language, relationships and sometimes even their sense of identity. Sarala Sapkota, 48, went through much the same experience after moving to Spain. Having worked as a nurse in Nepal for years, she arrived in Barcelona and began rebuilding her professional life in a new language and an unfamiliar society.

As time passed, however, her concerns shifted from her own life to the next generation. Would Nepali children born in Spain grow up speaking Nepali? Would they learn to read and write it? Would they be able to speak to their grandparents in their own language?

The search for answers to these questions led her to start a small initiative that has now completed 12 years.

The Nepali language school in Barcelona began in 2014 with just five children. Today, classes are held every Saturday. Hundreds of children have attended over the years, and around 40 are currently learning Nepali.

Sapkota is not the school’s principal classroom teacher. Her work happens largely behind the scenes — recruiting teachers, bringing parents together, finding a venue, organising programmes, resolving problems and, perhaps most importantly, ensuring that the school continues to operate.

That is why she is known in Barcelona’s Nepali community as the coordinator of the Nepali language school.

Her 12-year journey is about more than a school. It is the story of an immigrant community’s sustained effort to keep the next generation connected to its language, cultural heritage and ancestral roots.

From nursing to life as a migrant

Sarala Sapkota spent her childhood in Rayale, Kavre, now part of Ward No. 1 of Panauti Municipality. Her father ran a small shop, and she grew up as one of five children. She enjoyed studying, although school life in the village also meant that students had to take responsibility for everyday school activities.

She began her education at Shanti Niketan Lower Secondary School before moving to Kushadevi Secondary School, where she completed her School Leaving Certificate (SLC).

After the SLC, she tried studying law in Kathmandu. But the practical difficulties of living away from home and pursuing her education eventually brought that path to an end. She then chose nursing. After completing her studies at Maharajgunj Nursing Campus, she worked as a nurse in Nepal for around eight years.

After getting married, she moved to Spain in April 2005.

Barcelona was not the city with a sizeable Nepali population that it is today. Sapkota remembers there being only around 50 Nepalis in the city at the time. The community was small, and people knew one another well. New arrivals were invited into people’s homes, community members shared one another’s joys and hardships, and everyone helped where they could.

But Sarala Sapkota, like many migrants, was also trying to rebuild her own life in a new country.

She continued working as a nurse in Spain, spending around six years working in residential care facilities. She learned workplace practices from her local colleagues, but the language was a challenge.

“I realised that knowing the language was essential to becoming part of society here,” she recalls.

Her experience taught her that having professional skills was not enough when moving abroad. One also had to understand a new society, learn a new language and be willing to acknowledge what one did not know.

Perhaps that experience made her more conscious of the language her own children would grow up speaking. She could see that, although Nepali was spoken at home, her children’s wider world was taking shape in Spanish and Catalan.

The question was no longer just a personal one. How could the Nepali community preserve its language for the next generation?

An initiative that stalled, but an idea that endured

Between 2009 and 2011, Sarala Sapkota served on the executive committee of the Non-Resident Nepali Association (NRNA) in Spain. During that period, discussions began about teaching Nepali to children growing up abroad.

An attempt was made to organise weekly classes, but regular attendance proved difficult. On some occasions, only two children turned up out of the seven who had been expected. Eventually, the initiative stalled.

Sapkota, however, did not abandon the idea. For her, the question remained unanswered.

During the Christmas holidays in 2013, a meeting at the home of her friend Nita brought the idea back to life. Their children were playing together when the conversation once again turned to Nepali language classes.

This time, they decided not to wait for someone else to take the initiative.

“We started it ourselves,” Sapkota says.

The Nepali language school opened in the first week of 2014 with five children. The first classes were held at the home of Keshari Shrestha Nemkul, who took charge of teaching. Sapkota focused on management and coordination, helping form a team to oversee the school.

The number of students gradually increased. Before long, 22 children were attending classes at the house. Space became a problem, and the children had to be divided into two groups.

The school soon grew beyond the classroom and textbooks.

Celebrations of Dashain and Tihar became part of its activities. Children began appearing on stage in Nepali traditional dress, singing songs, reciting poems and performing the national anthem. When one family saw its child on stage in Nepali attire, another family was encouraged to enrol its own child.

The school continued to grow, but increasing enrolment was not Sapkota’s greatest challenge. Keeping the initiative going was.

“Starting something is easy, but continuing it is difficult,” she says.

From a room at home to a public community centre

In February 2016, the school moved to the NRNA office. Later, an opportunity arose to work with Centre Cívic Sedeta, a civic centre in Barcelona. What began as an arrangement for a few months continued for years.

Today, Nepali classes are held there every Saturday, with the venue provided free of charge.

For an immigrant community, securing space in a local public institution to teach its children their heritage language is an achievement in itself. But finding a venue is one thing; earning and maintaining trust is another.

According to Sapkota, the school gradually built that trust through its conduct and consistency.

“Over time, our behaviour helped us earn their trust,” she says.

The community behind the school

The school has never been the work of Sarala Sapkota alone. Over the years, more than a dozen volunteer teachers have contributed their time. Some taught for a few months, while others stayed for years. Parents brought their children every Saturday and supported school activities and events. Other members of the community offered help whenever it was needed.

Sapkota herself continued to oversee many aspects of the school, from deciding which teacher would take a particular class to coordinating with parents. She helped prepare programmes, arrange venues and resolve problems whenever they arose. If a child stopped attending regularly, she would speak with the parents to understand why.

Her role became less that of a classroom teacher and more that of a coordinator and guardian of the school.

“This has not been my effort alone,” she says. “Many teachers, parents and members of the community have given their time.”

Perhaps that is why the school has grown beyond an individual’s initiative to become a shared space for the community.

More than a language, a connection to their roots

Around 40 children, aged between four and 12 or 13, are currently learning Nepali at the school. Hundreds have attended over the years, although not all have stayed. Some families have moved elsewhere, while others have seen their children grow into teenagers, with schoolwork, friendships and new interests making it harder to attend Saturday classes regularly.

Yet the school has taught children much more than the Nepali alphabet.

They learn to read, write and speak Nepali. They sing songs, recite poems and deliver speeches in the language. They learn about Dashain, Tihar and Nepali culture. They are also encouraged to explore their family histories — which district in Nepal their family comes from, which village their parents grew up in, and where their grandparents’ homes are located.

For Sarala Sapkota, language and culture cannot be separated.

“Teaching the language alone is not enough. Children must also understand their culture and their roots,” she says.

Sometimes, the impact of the school becomes apparent not in the classroom, but when children travel to Nepal.

A child may read a signboard in Nepali on the street, recognise the name of their ancestral village or speak to their grandparents in Nepali. When parents share such experiences with Sapkota, she feels that the school’s purpose is gradually being fulfilled.

For her, recognising Nepali letters is only part of the achievement. It is also about helping children recognise a part of their own family and identity.

Today’s students, tomorrow’s teachers

After 12 years with the school, Sarala Sapkota’s dream is not to remain at its centre forever. She wants the children studying there today to take responsibility for it in the future.

She hopes today’s students will become tomorrow’s teachers, manage the school and pass the language on to the next generation.

“I want it to continue even after we step away,” she says.

That aspiration gives her work a significance beyond keeping weekly classes running. She has helped establish a foundation that the next generation can take forward in its own hands.

A class that began in a room at someone’s home now meets every Saturday in a public community centre in Barcelona.

Teachers have changed. Students and families have come and gone. Some children have grown up, while others have moved elsewhere. Yet the school has continued.

Perhaps that is the greatest measure of Sapkota’s 12 years of work.

Preserving a language abroad does not always begin with a large institution, a substantial budget or a major campaign. Sometimes, it begins with five children and a class in someone’s living room. When a small initiative is nurtured and sustained over the years, it can become a lasting inheritance for an entire generation.

Those Nepali letters carry more than a language. They hold memories of home, the names of ancestral villages, cultural traditions and the roots being passed from one generation to the next.

For 12 years, Sarala Sapkota has been helping keep those roots alive in Barcelona.

title: Nepal government’s film grant scheme gets mixed reviews - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal government’s film grant scheme gets mixed reviews  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
On Tuesday, the Nepal government announced a grant of Rs35 million in the current fiscal year to encourage the production of films that highlight the country’s culture, history and tourism. The Ministry of Information and Communication invited applications for the grant under the ‘Procedure for Providing Incentive Grants for Film Production in Areas of Cultural and National Significance, 2026’. It provided a 21-day deadline for the applications.

The grants are available in three categories: scriptwriting, production and post-production. The ministry will offer up to Rs500,000 each for five scripts, Rs7 million each for three film productions and Rs2 million each for five post-production projects. The initiative is part of the ministry’s approved programme for the 2026-27 fiscal year to support the development and promotion of Nepali cinema.

But filmmakers say the short notice leaves too little time to develop strong proposals.

Actress Nisha Adhikari questioned both the short application window and the decision to run the programme through the ministry rather than the Film Development Board.

“First, the programme should have been run through the Film Development Board,” she wrote on Facebook. “And what can anyone prepare in 21 days?”

Speaking to Kantipur, Adhikari welcomed the government’s decision to provide grants but criticised the way the scheme had been announced, saying the information could have been communicated more clearly and the deadline could have been realistic.

“The grant announcement should have been clearer and easier to understand,” she said. “The ministry could also have worked with the Film Development Board to plan the initiative for the entire year.”

Adhikari said creative work should not be rushed at the expense of quality.

Quality filmmaking takes time and the short deadline could discourage newcomers while favouring those who had already developed their scripts, she added.

Film producer and distributor Pradeep Kumar Udaya also questioned the decision to administer the programme through the ministry. In a Facebook post on Wednesday, he said the Film Development Board should have handled the initiative. He noted that the board had previously distributed grants under similar programmes and ran an initiative called Story Board.

“Why didn’t the ministry allocate the budget to the Film Development Board and let it run the programme?” he wrote on Facebook.

Udaya also expressed concern about the limited time available to prepare and submit scripts.

A scene from Min Bahadur Bham’s ‘Kalo Pothi’ (2015). The film was set in picturesque Mugu and brought to screen a story from wartime Nepal. It won several international and national awards. Courtesy of 'Kalo Pothi' film

Actor and film director Ashant Sharma also called out the announcement bluntly. “If this is true, it is corruption!” he wrote on social media. “What can anyone prepare in 21 days?”

Sharma said films exploring Nepal’s history, culture and tourism require extensive field research, including visits to locations and conversations with local people.

“Preparing a script and doing even the basic groundwork can take three to four months,” he said.

He argued that the short deadline would favour filmmakers with scripts already in development and disadvantage newcomers. While welcoming the government’s initiative to support cinema, he said the application process was impractical.

Film producer Ram Krishna Pokharel likewise welcomed the grant scheme but said the short deadline and lack of advance notice had made the process disorderly. He said the programme should have been announced well in advance and included in the government’s annual calendar to give filmmakers time to prepare.

“Had this been announced publicly when the budget was being prepared, interested filmmakers and other stakeholders could have planned,” he said. “The process needs to be made more practical.”

Meanwhile, Rakesh Gurung, an undersecretary in the ministry’s Audiovisual and Broadcasting Section, defended the government’s move. He said the 21-day deadline was for applications, not completed scripts, and could be extended if the response was insufficient.

“Some applicants may already have scripts ready, while others can develop them in stages after applying,” he said. “If we do not receive enough applications, we will extend the deadline.”

Ministry spokesperson Bishnu Koirala acknowledged that the programme could have shortcomings because it was being implemented for the first time, but said the ministry could revise the process in response to feedback.

title: Making Content Creators Responsible - The Rising Nepal
description: Making Content Creators Responsible  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
As the digital age advances, the fine line between content creators, influencers and journalists is becoming increasingly important. Almost every day, institutions such as the Press Council of Nepal and the Cyber Bureau of the Nepal Police receive complaints about misinformation, disinformation and cyber harassment targeting individuals and affecting their private and public lives. When complaints fall within the jurisdiction of either institution, legal processes can be initiated. However, both struggle when their hands are tied by a lack of laws to address genuine complaints or protect freedom of the press and the right to expression.

The time has now come to clearly draw a line between the two and amend or promulgate laws to correctly identify issues and take action. The Press Council was established long before social media platforms, which have become a major source of content creation and mass communication, began operating and gaining popularity. As a result, the Council is not equipped with the jurisdiction to address several forms of misinformation and disinformation spread through these platforms, which are here to stay and need to be taken seriously. It is also important to ensure that content creators become more responsible about what they share, as their content can go viral and reach a much larger audience than news disseminated by mainstream journalists.

Content creator landscape

According to the report Behind the Screens in Nepal, produced by UNESCO in 2026 and recently released in Lalitpur, the study is one of the few structured assessments of the country's digital content creator landscape. It states that the sector is strongly youth-driven, with 73.4 per cent of respondents aged 18–35. TikTok and Instagram were used by 72.7 per cent of the surveyed content creators. The report mentions that 36.7 per cent of respondents reported taking no action when they encountered misinformation, 26.6 per cent had experienced hate speech, and 25 per cent reported trolling or doxxing.

The report states that content creators have become central to Nepal's digital information ecosystem. However, their knowledge of fact-checking and pursuing legal recourse when they produce misinformation or disinformation, or become victims of it, remains limited. Some 53.1 per cent of respondents were unaware of whether the legal system supported their work. The report also mentions that ethical practices and sponsorship disclosures remain uneven, indicating that content creators may require guidance and training. As the number of content creators in Nepal grows, it is important to equip them with the knowledge and skills to fact-check information and produce ethical content so that they become more responsible for what they share.

It is a fact that Nepal's digital landscape is growing rapidly. Data shows that by late 2025, Nepal had 16.6 million internet users, accounting for 56 per cent of the total population. There were 14.8 million social media users. According to the Cyber Bureau, nearly 19,000 cybercrime cases were registered in the fiscal year 2024/25. These included harassment, sextortion, hate speech, and the misuse of photographs and videos.

Currently, there are two types of content creators. The most common are those who produce and share information, entertainment, or educational material, including videos, blogs, podcasts, graphics and social media posts across digital platforms. This helps them expand their outreach and reach a wider audience as their popularity grows. It can also help them establish a regular source of income. Many young people around the world follow this trend. They usually take information that is already available and share it in ways that their followers can easily consume. These content creators do not always fact-check or consider whether the information they share meets ethical standards. They are also often unregistered. Therefore, if they become sources of misinformation or disinformation or cause online harassment, it can be difficult for institutions such as the Press Council to take action.

The second type falls under the category of content creator journalism. These are trained journalists or individuals who independently produce journalistic work or provide their services to employers. They are responsible individuals who follow the basic principles of journalism and fact-check their content before publishing it. They are also contributing to the growth of the "creator economy" by distributing content across various platforms. These creator-model journalists adhere to journalistic standards of accountability, transparency, truth and fairness. There is also a group of individuals who have started operating in a "stunt" fashion. They barge into people's homes and offices, enter private and public places, capture audio and visual material, and publish parts of it without verifying what is correct and what is not.

Lack knowledge

While interacting with some influencers, it becomes clear that they lack knowledge of the basic principles of journalism. In fact, many people in Nepal confuse journalists with influencers. If we examine the flow of information during the recent Bhotekoshi flood, we can see that mainstream media practised responsible journalism by covering both human-interest stories and the technical aspects of such disasters. However, at the same time, several influencers shared videos that were unrelated to the disaster, along with other viral information that required correction.

Globally, content creators are here to stay. In Nepal, young people are becoming increasingly reliant on digital platforms for information. While interacting with a few influencers, it is clear that they are motivated to share factual information but lack the necessary fact-checking skills. It is important to build on this interest and guide them towards becoming factual and responsible content creators. It is also important for lawmakers to incorporate provisions into the upcoming Press Council Bill and Mass Media Bill that clarify how the Press Council can monitor social media. While monitoring mass media to promote ethical practices, it is equally important to ensure that freedom of the press and freedom of expression are protected.





(Sharma is a senior journalist and rights advocate. namrata1964@yahoo.com X handle: NamrataSharmaP)

title: What Steps Entail After FRLD Decision - The Rising Nepal
description: What Steps Entail After FRLD Decision  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Nepal’s success in getting support from the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) recently marks an important achievement in the realm of climate diplomacy. The Fund’s decision to provisionally set aside US$21.6 million for Nepal following the devastating Bhotekoshi floods offers recognition of the disproportionate burden that climate-vulnerable countries bear despite contributing relatively little to global greenhouse gas emissions. Yet, this diplomatic achievement is only the beginning of much larger tasks to follow.

The scale of the reconstruction challenge is enormous. Nepal’s Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment estimates recovery and reconstruction requirements at approximately Rs. 723.31 billion. The proposed Loss and Damage Fund assistance is therefore an appreciable contribution. But it represents only a small part of the overall requirement. The government must now move beyond celebrating the decision. It must establish a comprehensive strategy to translate international solidarity into tangible results on the ground.

Immediate priority

The immediate priority is to complete the procedures necessary to access the FRLD-allocated resources. The government should prepare a technically sound, result-oriented funding proposal in accordance with the implementation modalities. The proposal should clearly identify the intended beneficiaries, priority reconstruction activities, implementation arrangements, expected outcomes, and mechanisms for financial accountability. It should be firmly grounded in the Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment, verified local needs and the government’s recovery priorities. Particular attention should be given to restoring essential public services, rehabilitating damaged infrastructure and helping affected households recover their homes and livelihoods.

Nepal must also clarify the appropriate channel for receiving and administering the funds. Where permitted by the Fund’s rules, the government should create arrangements that strengthen national ownership and public financial management. Alternatively, it should work through an eligible accredited institution if that is required for access. The objective should be to avoid unnecessary administrative delays without compromising fiduciary standards, transparency or accountability. A dedicated inter-ministerial task force could oversee proposal preparation, resolve procedural bottlenecks and maintain regular communication with the Fund’s Board and secretariat. Given the urgency of reconstruction, the government should establish a clear timetable for completing each procedural step.

The matter of utmost priority is to develop a comprehensive national reconstruction and recovery framework. International assistance should not be mobilised through disconnected projects or competing institutional arrangements. Instead, Nepal needs a unified programme that brings together the federal government, provincial governments, local governments, development partners, the private sector and affected communities. Priority should be accorded to schools, health facilities, roads, bridges, drinking-water systems, irrigation networks, and electricity infrastructure, and damaged settlements. Support for displaced families, small businesses, farmers and other affected livelihood groups must form an integral part of the programme.

Reconstruction must not simply reproduce the vulnerabilities that contributed to the scale of the disaster. Infrastructure should be rebuilt according to updated hazard assessments, appropriate engineering standards and land-use planning. Where rebuilding in the same location would expose communities to unacceptable risks, safer alternatives should be explored through consultation and fair rehabilitation arrangements. Nepal cannot depend on a single international climate finance mechanism to meet its reconstruction needs. It must adopt a diversified resource mobilisation strategy that combines domestic financing, concessional international assistance, climate funds, private investment and community participation.

The federal budget should establish a dedicated reconstruction and resilience financing window. Resources can be mobilised through expenditure reprioritisation, savings from low-priority programme contingency allocations and carefully assessed additional domestic revenue measures. Second, Nepal should approach multilateral development banks, including the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank, for additional concessional financing, grants and technical assistance. In the meeting held with Finance Minister Dr. Swornim Wagle recently, the World Bank has already indicated that up to US$170 million in emergency financing is available to support the immediate response and restoration of critical infrastructure and services. Nepal should coordinate this support with other commitments to ensure that additional resources address identified financing gaps rather than duplicate existing assistance.

Bilateral development partners, the United Nations system, and the European Union should also be approached with a clear and concrete reconstruction programme. Nepal’s case must be presented not merely as an appeal for humanitarian sympathy but as a compelling investment in sustainable development and climate justice. Moreover, Nepal should explore the complementary use of other climate finance mechanisms, including the Green Climate Fund and the Adaptation Fund, wherever their eligibility requirements and mandates permit. These mechanisms should finance appropriate adaptation and resilience components.

The government should also use international climate negotiations to advocate for predictable, additional and accessible grant-based climate finance for vulnerable countries. Nepal’s experience could help demonstrate why existing financing arrangements need to respond more rapidly to catastrophic climate events. The private sector can contribute significantly to reconstruction, particularly in hydropower, telecommunications, transport, housing, renewable energy and resilient infrastructure. Public-private partnerships may be appropriate for commercially viable projects, provided that risks are allocated transparently and essential services remain affordable.

Diaspora initiatives

Nepali communities abroad can also contribute through structured diaspora initiatives, transparent fundraising mechanisms and partnerships with local organisations. Corporate contributions and charitable donations should complement, rather than replace, the government’s responsibility to provide essential services and protect vulnerable citizens. All contributions should be recorded through a transparent financing framework to prevent duplication and ensure that resources reach the intended beneficiaries.

Disaster recovery is also a test of Nepal’s federal governance system. The federal government must provide strategic direction, national standards and financial coordination, while provincial governments should coordinate regional infrastructure and technical support. Local governments are best placed to identify household-level needs, verify damage, prioritise schools and health facilities, and monitor implementation. A functional intergovernmental coordination mechanism should regularly review progress, resolve jurisdictional disputes and address financing gaps.





(The author is presently associated with Policy Research Institute (PRI) as a senior research fellow. rijalmukti@gmail.com)

title: Nepal announces 35 million rupees in grants for cultural films — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal announces 35 million rupees in grants for cultural films — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
The Government of Nepal has announced a 35 million rupee grant programme in the current fiscal year to support films highlighting the country’s culture, history and tourism potential. The Ministry of Information and Communications is accepting applications under the procedure for providing incentive grants for film production in areas of cultural and national significance, Kathmandu Post reports.

Three funding areas

The funds will be distributed among three categories: screenplay writing, film production and post-production. Up to 500,000 rupees will be allocated for each of five screenplays, up to 7 million rupees for each of three film projects, and up to 2 million rupees for each of five projects at the post-production stage.

The programme was included in the ministry’s approved plan for the 2026–2027 fiscal year, aimed at developing and promoting Nepali cinema. Applicants were given 21 days to submit their applications.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Filmmakers criticise the timeframe

Actress Nisha Adhikari and producer and distributor Pradeep Kumar Udaya said that the programme should have been administered by the Film Development Board, which had previously distributed grants under similar initiatives. They also criticised the short period for preparing applications.

Actor and director Ashant Sharma stressed that screenplays about Nepal’s history, culture and tourism require field research, trips to locations and communication with local residents. According to him, preparing a screenplay and carrying out basic preparatory work may take three to four months. Producer Ram Krishna Pokharel also called for such programmes to be announced in advance so that participants can plan their work.

Rakesh Gurung, deputy secretary of the ministry’s audiovisual and broadcasting division, responded that the 21 days were intended for submitting applications, not for creating completed screenplays. He added that the deadline could be extended if there were not enough applications. Ministry spokesperson Bishnu Koirala said that the Film Development Board would lead the programme’s implementation and provide technical recommendations, while the ministry would be responsible for budget matters.
